\chapter{Not One, Not a Scrap}
\label{ch:ge-negation}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I have none of a thing, choose correctly between German's two negatives, and put the second one where the sentence wants it.}

Every noun the book owns is cancelled and every verb it owns is refused, in one pass: the six things on the table, the household, the four words on the face, and the verbs. The chapter costs two new words and one welded ending, because kein is ein with two letters on the front and keinen carries the -en that the einen lesson already handed over as a bare word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kein]{kein — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} and the two words hiding inside it}

\label{lesson:GE-C32-kein}



\begin{quote}
Say the four words that closed the last chapter — \textbf{Arm, Finger, Fuß, Herz} — and then say \textbf{nicht} and \textbf{eins}. Two of those six are about to be welded together.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the four words for what is on your face — \emph{Auge, Ohr, Mund, Nase}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: kein}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{kein} — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}not a,\textquotedblright{} in front of a \emph{der}-word or a \emph{das}-word.
\end{quote}

Said \emph{kine}, rhyming with English \emph{mine}: the \textbf{ei} is the \emph{eye} sound you have had since \textbf{eins}, and the final \textbf{n} is plain.

Where you would say \textbf{ein}, say \textbf{kein} to cancel it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ein Hund} $\to$ \textbf{kein Hund} — \textquotedblleft{}a dog\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}no dog\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ein Brot} $\to$ \textbf{kein Brot} — \textquotedblleft{}a loaf\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}no loaf\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Nothing else in the phrase moves. The \textbf{k} goes on the front of the word you already have, and the noun stands exactly as it stood.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{kein} is Old High German \emph{\textbf{nihein}}, which is \textbf{ni} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{ein} (\textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}). \emph{Not one.} The \emph{ni-} wore down to nothing over a thousand years and left the \emph{k} that had crept in beside it, and the modern word no longer looks like its own parts.

English did the identical thing with its own two words, and English still shows the seam:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the pieces} & \textbf{what they made} \\
\midrule
\emph{ne} + \emph{ān} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}) & \textbf{nān} $\to$ \textbf{none}, \textbf{no} \\
\emph{ni} + \emph{ein} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}) & \textbf{nihein} $\to$ \textbf{kein} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{\textquotedblleft{}kein Brot\textquotedblright{}} and \emph{\textquotedblleft{}no bread\textquotedblright{}} are the same sentence, built twice out of the same two ideas by two languages doing it separately.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kein\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kine}, rhyming with English \emph{mine}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}ein Hund\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}kein Hund\textquotedblright{}
  \item it with food — \textquotedblleft{}kein Brot\textquotedblright{}
  \item it with the body words from the last chapter — \textquotedblleft{}kein Arm\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}kein Finger\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two pieces, then the word — \textquotedblleft{}ni … ein … kein\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ein Hund, kein Hund.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word does \emph{kein} cancel? (\emph{\textbf{ein}}.) What two pieces are inside it? (\textbf{Ni} and \textbf{ein}.) Which English word was built from the same two? (\textbf{None}.) Which body word from the last chapter shows Grimm's \emph{p $\to$ f}? (\emph{\textbf{Fuß}}.) Next: \emph{kein} in front of a \emph{die}-word.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[keine]{keine — the same word, in front of a \emph{die}}

\label{lesson:GE-C32-keine}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kein Hund.} Now do the same to \textbf{eine Katze} before you read on. You already know the answer; you learned it on \emph{ein} and \emph{eine} long ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: keine}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{keine} — the shape \emph{kein} takes in front of a \emph{die}-word.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{eine Katze} $\to$ \textbf{keine Katze} — \textquotedblleft{}a cat\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}no cat\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{eine Nacht} $\to$ \textbf{keine Nacht} — \textquotedblleft{}a night\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}no night\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

And it is the shape in front of a \textbf{plural}, whatever the noun's own gender, because a German plural takes \emph{die}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{keine Hände} — \textquotedblleft{}no hands\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The extra \textbf{-e} is not a new ending. It is \emph{eine}'s \textbf{-e}, unmoved. Put the \emph{k} on the front of the word you already say and stop there.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one word cancels the whole family}]
Something worth noticing before the next lesson complicates it: German gets \textbf{two} jobs out of these two shapes. \emph{Keine Katze} is \textquotedblleft{}no cat\textquotedblright{} — one cat, and there is not one. \emph{Keine Hände} is \textquotedblleft{}no hands\textquotedblright{} — however many there might have been, there are none.

English needs \emph{no} for the first and \emph{no} for the second and \emph{not any} for a third case, and never had to decide which; German lets the noun's own article decide it, so there is nothing extra to remember.

Mass words take \emph{kein} and \emph{keine} too, on the same reasoning — \textbf{die Milch} is a \emph{die}-word, so:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich habe keine Milch.} — \textquotedblleft{}I have no milk.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}eine Katze\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}keine Katze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other pair, from the chapter before — \textquotedblleft{}ein Hund, kein Hund\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a mass word — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Milch.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a face word — \textquotedblleft{}keine Nase\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a plural — \textquotedblleft{}keine Hände\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sentence everyone says — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape goes in front of \emph{Katze}, and why? (\emph{\textbf{Keine}} — \emph{Katze} is a \emph{die}-word, so it takes \emph{eine}, so it takes \emph{keine}.) Which shape goes in front of a plural? (\emph{\textbf{Keine}}, because every German plural takes \emph{die}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I have no time.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich habe keine Zeit}.) Next: what happens when the thing you do not have is the \emph{object} of \emph{haben}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[keinen]{keinen — for the thing you do \emph{not} have}

\label{lesson:GE-C32-keinen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I have a brother\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Ich habe einen Bruder}. That lesson handed you \emph{einen} as a single word and promised the system behind it would come later. Some of it arrives now, and it costs nothing, because you are about to watch a word you met yesterday do the identical thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: keinen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{keinen} — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}not a,\textquotedblright{} for a \emph{der}-word that is the thing being had.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich habe einen Bruder.} $\to$ \textbf{Ich habe keinen Bruder.}
\end{quote}

The \emph{-en} is the one from \emph{einen}, unchanged. You are not learning a second ending; you are watching the ending you already own ride along on the negative word, because \emph{kein} is \emph{ein} with two letters welded to the front and nothing else touched.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three shapes, and the one that moves}]
Line the three up against what they stand in front of and one thing jumps out:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{in front of} & \textbf{naming it} & \textbf{having it} \\
\midrule
a \emph{der}-word (\emph{Hund}) & \textbf{kein} Hund & \textbf{keinen} Hund \\
a \emph{die}-word (\emph{Schwester}) & \textbf{keine} Schwester & \textbf{keine} Schwester \\
a \emph{das}-word (\emph{Brot}) & \textbf{kein} Brot & \textbf{kein} Brot \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the \emph{der} line changes. \emph{Die} and \emph{das} words look identical whether they are the thing doing or the thing done to — which is why you have got this far without meeting the question at all, and why \emph{einen} could be handed over as a plain word for twenty-three chapters.

That is the whole of what German asks of you here, and it is much less than the reputation suggests: \textbf{one line out of three moves, and it is the \emph{der} line.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe einen Bruder\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Bruder\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the broken forms of \emph{haben} — \textquotedblleft{}du hast keinen Hund\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}er hat keinen Hund\textquotedblright{}
  \item the drink that is a \emph{der}-word — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the drink that is a \emph{der}-word too — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Tee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \emph{die}-word, which does not move — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Schwester.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Bruder und keine Schwester.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three shapes changes when the noun is the thing being had? (Only the \emph{\textbf{der}} one — \emph{kein} becomes \emph{keinen}.) Where have you seen that \emph{-en} before? (On \emph{\textbf{einen}}, in \emph{ich habe einen Bruder}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I have no brother and no sister.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich habe keinen Bruder und keine Schwester.}) Next: which negative word to reach for when there is no noun to cancel.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kein oder nicht]{kein oder nicht — picking the right one}

\label{lesson:GE-C32-kein-oder-nicht}



\begin{quote}
You now own two words that both mean \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}. Say them: \textbf{kein} and \textbf{nicht}. German makes you choose, and the choosing turns out to be mechanical.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the two words for what you hear with and what you eat with — \emph{Ohr} and \emph{Mund}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one cancels a noun, one cancels the rest}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{kein} goes in front of a noun that would otherwise have carried \emph{ein}. \textbf{nicht} cancels anything else at all.
\end{quote}

Test it by asking whether \emph{ein} could stand where you are about to negate. If it could, reach for \emph{kein}; if it could not, reach for \emph{nicht}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich habe keinen Hund.} — no \emph{Hund}. A noun, so \emph{kein}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist nicht gut.} — nothing to put \emph{ein} in front of. \emph{Gut} is a quality, so \emph{nicht}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich verstehe nicht.} — the verb itself is what fails. \emph{Nicht}.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The two words are cousins, and knowing it makes the split easier to hold. Both begin life as the ancient negative particle \textbf{ni}, and each picked up a different second half:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ni} + \textbf{ein} (\textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{nihein} $\to$ \textbf{kein}, which cancels \emph{a thing}.
  \item \textbf{ni} + a word meaning \emph{a whit, a scrap} $\to$ \textbf{niwiht} $\to$ \textbf{nicht}, which cancels \emph{anything at all}.
\end{itemize}

English ran the same fork: \emph{ne} + \emph{ān} gave \textbf{none}, \emph{ne} + \emph{ā-wiht} gave \textbf{naught} and then \textbf{not}. The choice is a fossil of what each word once counted.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say which negative each one wants, out loud, before you say the sentence.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a noun, so \emph{kein} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Hund.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a quality, so \emph{nicht} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin nicht müde.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a verb, so \emph{nicht} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich verstehe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a noun, so \emph{kein} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a verb, so \emph{nicht} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich schlafe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three verbs of the body at rest, all cancelled — \textquotedblleft{}ich sitze nicht, ich stehe nicht, ich schlafe nicht\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Hund. Ich bin nicht müde.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What question decides the choice? (Could \emph{\textbf{ein}} have stood there? If yes, \emph{kein}; if no, \emph{nicht}.) Which one cancels a quality? (\emph{\textbf{Nicht}}.) Which ancient word starts both of them? (\emph{\textbf{Ni}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I do not understand.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich verstehe nicht.}) Next: where in the sentence that \emph{nicht} has to stand.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nicht am Ende]{nicht am Ende — where the \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} goes}

\label{lesson:GE-C32-nicht-stellung}



\begin{quote}
You can pick the right negative. Now the last piece of this chapter: German is fussy about \emph{where} \textbf{nicht} stands, and the fussiness has one cause you can see through.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it stands in front of what it cancels}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{nicht} stands \textbf{immediately in front of the word it cancels} — and when what it cancels is the verb itself, there is nothing in front of it to stand before, so it goes to the \textbf{end}.
\end{quote}

Both halves of that are one habit, seen from two sides:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Das ist nicht gut.} — the quality is cancelled, so \emph{nicht} leads it.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich wohne nicht in Berlin.} — the place is cancelled, so \emph{nicht} leads it.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich verstehe nicht.} — the verbing is cancelled. There is no word left to lead, and \emph{nicht} falls to the far end.
\end{quote}

English parks its \emph{not} beside the helper verb and leaves it — \emph{I do not live in Berlin} — so German's \emph{nicht} sounds to an English ear as though it drifts. It is being aimed.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The end-of-sentence habit has a history. \textbf{Nicht} began as a \textbf{noun} — \emph{niwiht}, \textquotedblleft{}not a whit\textquotedblright{}, a scrap of a thing — and a German object goes late. So the old sentence was something like \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I understand not-a-scrap\textquotedblright{}}, with the scrap sitting where any object sits.

The meaning drained out of the noun and left the position behind. A separable prefix goes to that same far end, for a related reason: German finishes a sentence with the piece that completes its sense.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cancelling a quality — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item cancelling a place — \textquotedblleft{}Ich wohne nicht in Berlin.\textquotedblright{}
  \item cancelling the verb, so \emph{nicht} goes last — \textquotedblleft{}Ich verstehe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four verbs of taking things in and putting them out, each cancelled — \textquotedblleft{}ich höre nicht, ich sehe nicht, ich lese nicht, ich schreibe nicht\textquotedblright{}
  \item aim it, then move it — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht gut\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}Ich höre nicht\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich verstehe nicht. Das ist nicht gut.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{nicht} stand against an adjective? (\textbf{Straight in front} — \emph{nicht gut}.) Against the verb? (\textbf{At the end}.) What was \emph{nicht} before it was a negative? (A \textbf{noun}, \emph{niwiht}.) Say the three sentences.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Nichts davon — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:GE-R32-nichts-davon}



\begin{quote}
Two questions before you say anything. Which negative goes in front of a noun, and what decides which of its three shapes you use? Then: where does the other negative stand?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: everything on the table, cancelled}
Six things this book has put in front of you to eat and drink. Say each one's article first, then cancel it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{das} Brot $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}kein Brot\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{das} Wasser $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}kein Wasser\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{der} Wein $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}kein Wein\textquotedblright{}, and having it, \textquotedblleft{}keinen Wein\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{der} Kaffee $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}kein Kaffee\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}keinen Kaffee\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{der} Tee $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}kein Tee\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}keinen Tee\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{die} Milch $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}keine Milch\textquotedblright{}, which does not move
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the people and the face}
Now reach further back — the animals, the household, and the four words on your face. Nothing here is new; the negative in front of it is.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two animals — \textquotedblleft{}kein Hund\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}keine Katze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the household, having none of them — \textquotedblleft{}keinen Bruder, keine Schwester, keine Mutter, keinen Vater\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair the \emph{-in} suffix made — \textquotedblleft{}keinen Freund, keine Freundin\textquotedblright{}
  \item the collective — \textquotedblleft{}keine Familie\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four on your face — \textquotedblleft{}kein Auge, kein Ohr, keinen Mund, keine Nase\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of those four is a \emph{die}-word, and prove it by its negative — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{die} Nase, keine Nase\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the verbs, refused}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the verb cancelled, so \emph{nicht} goes last — \textquotedblleft{}Ich verstehe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the quality cancelled, so \emph{nicht} leads it — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist nicht gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin nicht müde.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the noun, so \emph{kein} — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{}
  \item both in one breath — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keine Zeit und ich verstehe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the three shapes and what each stands in front of. (\emph{\textbf{Kein}} before a \emph{der} or \emph{das} word, \emph{\textbf{keine}} before a \emph{die} word and every plural, \emph{\textbf{keinen}} before a \emph{der} word that is being had.) What two pieces is \emph{kein} built from? (\textbf{Ni} and \textbf{ein} — \textquotedblleft{}not one\textquotedblright{}.) And when does the other negative go to the end of the sentence? (When what it cancels is \textbf{the verb}.) Next: the question that has no question word in it.
\end{tcolorbox}
